hero.name: Mahesh
hero.who: a 47-year-old who runs his family's carton factory in Ludhiana through a crisis

story.b: Mahesh took over his father's carton factory in Ludhiana ten years ago. It has forty-two workers, two shifts and a reputation for reliable boxes. Then, in one phone call, the biggest client moves its orders to a cheaper supplier in Baddi. Overnight, almost half the order book disappears. Mahesh stays late in his cabin, reading management books he bought years ago. They talk about vision and growth. None of them tells him what to do when salaries are due in three weeks, when his oldest friend is his production head and is not coping, or when his workers keep glancing at his cabin door. The wall clock ticks. He feels completely alone with it.

ask.q: Mahesh keeps searching books for a clear formula to handle the crisis. What is the most useful shift for him?
o: Accept there is no perfect answer and start making the hard calls with what he knows
Keep reading until he finds a method that fits exactly
Wait a few weeks to see if the client comes back
ask.why: The hardest situations rarely have a formula, so searching for one becomes a way of delaying. Waiting hopes the problem will fix itself. Accepting that every choice will be imperfect lets him act now, while there is still time and money to steer.

chapters.take: Hard problems have no recipe. Decide with what you know, and act.

story.b: Gurpreet and Mahesh have been friends since school. Gurpreet runs production, but the new printing machines confuse him, and quality complaints have tripled. Mahesh has avoided the conversation for four months. Now, with the factory in trouble, he cannot avoid it any longer. He sets himself a deadline: decide by Friday. He thinks about the options. None of them is painless. On Friday evening, he takes Gurpreet for a walk along the canal and tells him the truth, kindly and directly. He offers him a role running dispatch and loading, where his calm way with drivers is a real strength. Gurpreet is hurt and silent for a long time. Then he says he will try.

ask.q: Mahesh has avoided the talk about his struggling friend for four months. What should he do now?
o: Wait for his friend to notice the problem himself
Quietly hire someone above him without explaining
Set a deadline, decide, and talk to his friend honestly and respectfully
ask.why: Waiting lets quality and trust slip further, and hiring around him silently is a betrayal that will come out anyway. There is no painless option, but a clear deadline forces a decision, and an honest, respectful talk protects both the factory and the friendship as much as possible.

chapters.take: When no option feels good, set a deadline and choose the most honest one.

story.b: Weeks pass. New orders are slow, a skilled machine operator leaves for a competitor, and Mahesh barely sleeps. He starts to believe that he alone is failing, that his father would have handled this better. His wife notices he has stopped eating properly. One Sunday, he drives to Jalandhar to meet an old family friend, a retired factory owner. Over chai at a roadside dhaba on the highway, he tells him everything. The older man listens, then says every business he knew went through stretches like this. Mahesh drives home lighter. That night he writes a short list of next useful moves: call three new clients, visit two online sellers who need boxes, cut material waste.

ask.q: Mahesh lies awake every night feeling he alone is failing. What would help most?
o: Hide it from everyone so nobody loses confidence
Talk to someone he trusts and focus on the next useful step
Work through the nights until things turn around
ask.why: Hiding the struggle makes it heavier, and working through nights burns out the person the factory needs most. Sharing with someone trusted reminds him that hard stretches are normal, and turning his energy to the next useful step keeps him moving instead of sinking.

chapters.take: Every leader faces dark stretches. Share the weight and take the next step.

story.b: The numbers are clear. Mahesh must close the night shift, and eight workers will lose their jobs. His accountant suggests putting up a notice and saying it is temporary, to avoid trouble. Mahesh refuses. That evening he gathers the whole night shift on the factory floor himself. He tells them plainly what happened, that it was his decision, and that he is sorry. He explains they will get their full dues and an extra month's pay. He has already called two other factory owners in the industrial area who need workers, and he hands out their numbers. He writes a reference for each person. Some are angry. But nobody says he lied to them.

ask.q: The accountant suggests informing the night shift workers through a notice board message. What should Mahesh do?
o: Tell them himself, explain honestly, take responsibility and help them leave with dignity
Use the notice, since it avoids an emotional scene
Tell them it is only temporary, to soften the blow
ask.why: A notice feels cold and makes him look like he is hiding, and calling it temporary when it is not is a lie people will remember. Telling them in person, owning the decision and supporting them through it keeps trust with those who stay and those who leave.

chapters.take: People can handle hard news. What they do not forgive is being misled.

story.b: In good years, Mahesh ran the factory by agreement. Long meetings, everyone's opinion heard, even on the canteen menu. Now his managers want to keep debating every change for hours. Mahesh realises this is not a normal time. It is a fight for survival. So he changes how he leads. Every morning at nine, a fifteen-minute meeting standing beside the machines. Three clear priorities: win online sellers as clients, cut waste, deliver every order on time. He makes quick decisions and explains them briefly. Some managers find it harsh. Five months later, when orders have steadied, he deliberately switches back, and starts asking workers for ideas again over tea.

ask.q: With orders halved, Mahesh's managers want long meetings to agree on every change. What should he do?
o: Keep the long meetings, since everyone must agree
Let each manager handle things their own way
Recognise this is a survival moment, and give clear, quick direction for now
ask.why: Agreement and freedom suit calm times, but in a crisis slow meetings can cost the factory its survival. Leaving everyone to their own way scatters effort. Recognising which mode he is in, and leading firmly until things stabilise, is what this moment needs.

chapters.take: Calm times and crisis times need different leaders. Know which one you are in.

story.b: As orders recover, mostly from online sellers, Mahesh looks back at what the crisis exposed. His supervisors had never been trained. They shouted when things went wrong because nobody had shown them another way. So he starts Saturday morning sessions on planning, quality and handling people. He also needs a new quality supervisor. One candidate is average at everything. Another, a woman from the packing line, spots defects that everyone else misses, but she speaks little English and has never managed anyone. Mahesh picks her and pairs her with an older supervisor for three months. He also makes one rule clear to everyone: no shouting on the floor. Complaints drop within weeks.

ask.q: Mahesh must pick a quality supervisor. One candidate is average at everything; another spots defects brilliantly but speaks little English. Whom should he choose?
o: The average candidate, since there is nothing to worry about
The one with the rare strength, and train her in what she lacks
Neither, and keep looking until someone perfect appears
ask.why: Hiring for the absence of weakness often gets someone who is fine but never excellent. Waiting for perfect leaves the job empty. A real strength in the core skill matters most, and training can fill the smaller gaps. Investing in people builds a team that lasts.

chapters.take: Strong teams come from hiring for strengths and training people well.

story.b: A year after the phone call, the factory runs with thirty-eight workers. Two from the old night shift have come back as orders grew, and they asked for Mahesh by name. Gurpreet runs dispatch, and the truck drivers love him. The new quality supervisor now trains others on the packing line. The Saturday sessions continue, and the shouting has mostly stopped. Mahesh still has hard days. Sometimes he still lies awake. But now he calls his friend in Jalandhar instead of staring at the ceiling, and he no longer looks for answers in books that were never written for days like these. He looks at his people and asks what the next useful step is.

chapters.take: Leading through hard times means honest calls, shared weight and real care for people.
